why: A jam together with an overfilled tray usually means the paper was loaded badly.
Loose guides let the stack shift and jam.
Torn pieces left inside block the paper path.
A jam message with nothing visible points to a small scrap blocking a sensor.
Damp or curled paper sticks and jams.
Damp paper wrinkles easily.
Misloaded paper is a common cause of any jam.
Leftover scraps are a common cause of any jam.
Pickup rollers wear out on older or heavily used printers.
If the tray is not overfilled, a dirty or worn pickup roller is the likely reason paper is not pulled in.
Damp or curled paper will not pick up well.
Several sheets feeding at once suggests the separation pad is not separating them.
Separation pads wear with age.
Damp paper sticks together.
Loose guides let the paper enter at an angle.
Crooked output most often comes from the paper guides.
On a laser printer wrinkles can come from a failing fuser.
Faded laser print with a low toner message means the toner is running out.
Faded laser print is most often low toner.
Draft or economy mode deliberately prints lighter.
Ink dries in the nozzles when an inkjet sits unused.
Faded inkjet print usually means clogged nozzles or low ink.
Lines on laser printouts often come from a dirty or damaged drum or cartridge.
Streaks with a low toner warning suggest the toner is nearly gone.
Lines on inkjet printouts are classic clogged nozzles.
Marks repeating at regular spacing point to a damaged drum.
A worn drum is likely on an old printer.
Ghost images can come from a worn drum.
Ghost images can also come from a failing fuser.
Toner that rubs off was not fused to the paper, so the fuser is failing.
Smudged inkjet print is often a wrong paper type or quality setting.
Ink smears on damp paper.
Smudged toner suggests poor fusing.
The protective seal on a new cartridge stops it printing.
Blank pages right after a cartridge change point to the seal or seating.
An empty toner cartridge gives blank pages.
Blank inkjet pages often mean an empty cartridge.
Dried nozzles after a long idle period give blank pages.
A low ink message with blank pages means the ink is empty.
Fully black laser pages point to a high-voltage fault.
A missing colour on an inkjet is usually a clogged nozzle or empty colour ink.
Wrong colours can come from greyscale or wrong settings.
The printer is reporting low toner.
The printer is reporting low ink.
An offline status is usually a setting on the computer.
With USB a bad cable or port can look like offline.
A wireless printer goes offline when the network link breaks.
A router change breaks the printer's connection.
If a USB printer is not detected, suspect the cable or port.
Updates often remove or break drivers.
A wireless printer not found usually lost its network.
A dropping Wi-Fi link is a signal or network setting problem.
Jobs that never print are usually stuck in the spooler.
Jobs queue up while the printer is offline.
A driver error means the driver is missing or corrupt.
The driver broke after an update.
Strange characters mean the printer cannot interpret the data it receives.
A faulty USB cable can corrupt data.
Slow printing is commonly caused by quality settings or large files.
A weak Wi-Fi link slows data transfer.
No power may be the supply, but the socket and cable must be ruled out.
With the socket and cable ruled out, the printer's own power supply has failed.
A warning light with no other symptoms needs a general reset and check.
The warning light is probably the jam sensor.
The printer cannot read the cartridge chip.
Refilled or clone cartridges often have chips the printer rejects.
A newly fitted cartridge may be mis-seated or the wrong model.
Grinding suggests worn gears or a mechanical fault.
Gears wear out with age and heavy use.
Noise with a jam usually means the rollers are fighting an obstruction.
Burning smell, smoke or extreme heat is a safety hazard.
The print head carriage is physically blocked.
On a dot matrix printer, faint print most often means the ribbon ink is used up.
Faint print with an old ribbon strongly points to a worn-out ribbon.
If a dot matrix printer sounds like it prints but nothing appears, the ribbon is usually not fitted properly.
A completely dry ribbon also leaves the page blank.
A line of dots missing through every character usually means a broken print head pin.
Missing dots with a loose ribbon point to the ribbon, not the head.
White horizontal lines on dot matrix print are a classic sign of a dead print head pin.
A loose or twisted ribbon causes missing or patchy characters.
Paper coming off the sprockets means the tractor or paper path is set up wrongly.
Most dot matrix jams come from continuous paper not sitting correctly on the tractor.
Crooked feeding on a dot matrix usually means misaligned sprocket holes or edge guides.
A thermal printer cannot print on paper that is not heat-sensitive.
Blank receipts on thermal paper usually mean the roll was put in backwards.
Blank receipts can also mean the roll is not thermal paper.
Faint receipts usually mean a dirty thermal head.
Pale bands on receipts come from residue on the thermal head.
The printer stops when the paper roll is finished.
The printer will not print while the roll cover is open.
A steady error light on a receipt printer usually means cover open or no paper.
A cutter error is usually caused by paper or an object caught in the cutter.
Receipt jams often happen at the auto-cutter.
Ink absorber and service life messages mean the waste ink pads are full.
A print head error message points to a failed or overheated print head.
A drum warning right after fitting a new drum means the counter was not reset.
A drum warning without a new drum means the drum is near the end of its life.
Brother's Drum ! message means the corona wire must be cleaned.
Streaks together with a Drum ! message point to a dirty corona wire.
A size or media mismatch message means the paper does not match the settings.
A fuser error means the fuser did not reach its working temperature.
A 49 service error or memory full message is usually caused by a print job the printer cannot handle.
The error after an update suggests a firmware or driver mismatch with the print job.
The waste toner box full message means the box must be replaced.
Skipping labels mean the media sensor is not calibrated for the labels loaded.
Media out with labels loaded usually means the sensor is misaligned or not calibrated.
Media out messages come mostly from label printers with an uncalibrated sensor.
A label printer reports out of paper when its sensor cannot see the labels.
Ribbon out means the ribbon is finished or not loaded correctly.
Blank labels usually mean wrong label type or labels or ribbon loaded the wrong way.
Faint labels usually mean a low darkness setting or a dirty print head.
White lines on labels come from dirt on the print head.
Blank pages right after refilling an ink tank point to air in the ink tubes.
Faint print after refilling means ink has not yet reached the print head.
Gaps and lines after refilling come from air bubbles in the ink path.
Office printers stop when a cover is not fully closed.
A no paper message with paper in the tray usually means it is loaded badly.
Brother and Pantum manuals both say a laser cartridge error or no cartridge detected usually means the cartridge is not seated correctly.
Phone printing fails mostly because of the network or the phone's print service.
A wireless printer the phone cannot see is usually on a different network.
A service call code means the machine found a fault that needs a technician.
Extra blank pages usually come from the document or the paper size setting.
Blank pages with several sheets feeding at once point to a worn separation pad.
Two-sided printing stops when the back cover or duplex tray is not closed or the size is unsupported.
Brother's guide says grey background shading comes from the drum unit or a hot, humid room.
Grey background on a heavily used printer points to a worn drum.
Random toner specks usually come from material stuck on the drum.
Label glue or staples leave material on the drum that prints as specks.
Marks repeating at the drum spacing after printing labels mean glue is stuck on the drum.
Toner on the back of pages comes from a dirty transfer roller or fuser.
Toner rubbing off envelopes or card usually means the media type or levers are wrong.
Creased envelopes mean the envelope levers or feed path are not set for envelopes.
Envelopes and thick paper jam when fed from the main tray instead of the manual slot.
A manual feed request means the print job chose the manual slot as its paper source.
A misaligned or too much skew message means the roll is not loaded straight.
Crooked output on a large-format printer usually comes from how the roll sits on the spindle.
Cassette errors on photo printers mean the ink and paper cassettes do not match or are not seated.
A blank photo print usually means the ink sheet is used up or the wrong size.
Bluetooth printing problems usually mean the pairing was lost or the app has no Bluetooth access.
A phone software update deletes stored Bluetooth pairings.
Print in the wrong place on the page points to page length or top-of-form settings.
On a dot matrix with continuous paper, the tractor page length setting must match the paper.
Large-format jams usually start with a roll that is skewed or loose.
A PCL XL or PostScript error page means the driver's print language does not suit the printer.
The error after an update suggests the driver was replaced with an unsuitable one.
Canon codes 1686 and 1688 mean the ink is out or its level cannot be read.
Refilled cartridges often stop the printer from reading the ink level.
Colour fringes mean the colour units are printing out of line.
On a colour laser, misaligned colours are fixed by colour registration.
Beeping usually signals a general error that a restart may clear.
Epson dot matrix printers beep five times for an error that needs a restart and a jam check.
Beeping with a jam usually means paper or a scrap is still inside.
